claims.text: Intermediate dwell periods during rapid thermal processing enhance atomic interdiffusion.
Intermediate dwell periods reduce kinetic trapping.
The modified temperature profile will suppress phase separation and elemental segregation and favor a uniform single-phase solid solution.
The modified temperature profile will improve nanoparticle morphology.
Rapidly heated and cooled noble metal–based HEA nanoparticles often exhibit phase separation, elemental segregation, and uncontrolled shapes because of kinetic trapping.
The controlled intervention is to reduce the overall heating ramp rate and introduce short intermediate isothermal dwell periods.
The relevant processing regime includes peak temperatures above 1100 K and cooling rates of approximately 10^4–10^5 K/s.
Rapid cooling can preserve a single-phase nanoparticle structure and small particle size.
Dwell duration must be limited to avoid nanoparticle coarsening or agglomeration.
Enhanced interdiffusion produces uniform nanoscale mixing and reduces local compositional fluctuations that lead to phase separation.
Additional time at elevated temperature increases atomic mobility and intermixing.
Increased atomic mobility minimizes kinetic trapping and promotes homogeneous nucleation of a single-phase alloy.
Secondary phases and segregated regions typically arise from ultra-rapid temperature changes.
Relative to rapid heating without a dwell, the modified profile will increase phase and compositional homogeneity while retaining a single-phase state.
The hypothesis applies to noble metal–based HEA nanoparticles containing more than five elements.
Excessively long dwell periods can cause excessive particle growth or coarsening.
Peak temperatures that are too low will not provide meaningful atomic mobility.
The optimal dwell duration and temperature are unknown and may vary with elemental combination and processing setup.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant improvement in phase homogeneity and segregation, or observation of coarsening or secondary phases, would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The intervention specifies reducing the overall heating ramp rate as well as adding dwell periods, whereas the proposed experiment describes retaining the same rapid heating and changing only the addition of dwell periods. Thus the tested intervention does not fully match the stated intervention.
